claims.claim: Novelist Natasha Pulley points out that Hobb declines the efficient move of simply naming the garden maid, and instead has two characters work out between them who she is.
claims.quote: which would have been the narratively efficient thing to do

claims.claim: Pulley's close reading turns on one concrete noun: Fitz disputes the Fool's simile 'hair the colour of clean straw' because straw belongs to his stable upbringing and not to the Fool's.
claims.quote: What’s brilliant, though, is that he does it over straw

claims.claim: Pulley reads a passing quarrel over a minor descriptive detail as carrying, without statement, the class histories of both speakers.
claims.quote: It says volumes about both of them

claims.feature: other: small-scale detail beside large-scale spectacle
claims.claim: Pulley contrasts the trilogy's dragons, prophets and sweeping landscapes with what she calls its pin-sharp moments.
claims.quote: but it has these pin-sharp moments too

claims.claim: Novelist Steven Erikson says what he admired on first reading Assassin's Apprentice was the controlled point of view and the leisurely pace.
claims.quote: admired the controlled point of view, the leisurely pace

claims.claim: Erikson reports that after the book's turning scene he reread the preceding pages line by line to find the hints Hobb had planted that he had missed.
claims.quote: deconstructing, line by line, to catch every subtle tell

claims.claim: Erikson says he sets the opening chapters of Assassin's Apprentice as required reading on point of view in the writing workshops he teaches.
claims.quote: I cite the opening chapters of Assassin’s Apprentice as required reading
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'To this day in the workshops'

claims.claim: Erikson describes the child point of view in fantasy as a device that delivers knowledge to the reader piecemeal at the child's rate of comprehension, in an essay whose worked example is Hobb's Fitz.
claims.quote: Knowledge is fed piecemeal, at a child’s pace of comprehension
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'It’s no accident the child POV'

claims.claim: Critic Adam Whitehead states the rule governing reliability in the Farseer narration: the further an event lies from Fitz's own perspective, the less reliable the account of it is.
claims.quote: the further things and events are from Fitz's perspective

claims.claim: Whitehead names a naturalistic manner of presenting the world, alongside characterisation, as Hobb's greatest strength.
claims.quote: her naturalistic way of presenting the world

claims.claim: Whitehead names as Hobb's greatest weakness a tendency to meander, with characters sitting and talking about the plot at length.
claims.quote: a tendency to meander, to have characters sitting around talking

claims.claim: Whitehead calls Hobb a superior prose writer and a gifted communicator of emotions and atmosphere.
claims.quote: Hobb is a superior prose writer and a gifted communicator
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'Hobb is a superior prose writer'

claims.claim: Hobb, in her own transcribed words, says a farmer and a character from a sailing-ship background will choose different vocabulary for the same things, and gives her own house as the example, where the same rooms are galley, head and deck to her sailor husband and kitchen, bathroom and floor to her.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (transcript)
claims.quote: we have a galley, we have a head, we have a deck
claims.page: second half, 'Well, again, it’s knowing the character’s background'

claims.claim: Hobb gives a test for per-speaker register: read a passage of dialogue and you should be able to tell who is speaking without the attribution tags.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (transcript)
claims.quote: you should be able to tell who is talking without
claims.page: second half, 'If you want to do a double check, read your dialogue'

claims.claim: Hobb names sentence length as one of the carriers of per-speaker difference, saying some characters speak in longer sentences and some in shorter ones, using The Lord of the Rings as her example.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (transcript)
claims.quote: Some characters speak in longer sentences, some speak in shorter sentences
claims.page: second half, 'If you have two farmers'

verdicts.trueWording: which would have been the narratively efficient thing to do
verdicts.note: Raw page reached (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200); full article body present. Quote exact. Every limb holds: 'But nobody just says ‘it was Garetha the garden maid’, which would have been the narratively efficient thing to do. Far more realistically — they live in a castle with hundreds of people in it — neither of them quite know who she is and they have to work it out between them.' Byline 'By Natasha Pulley', 'Published on July 10, 2015'; the author bio on the same page confirms novelist ('The Watchmaker of Filigree Street is her first novel').

verdicts.trueWording: What’s brilliant, though, is that he does it over straw
verdicts.note: Quote exact. All limbs on the page: the Fool says 'Hair the colour of clean straw'; Fitz answers 'Her hair is light brown, not gold'; Pulley then writes 'He grew up in stables and now he’s having to work as a manservant. The Fool, however, was the King’s jester and now lives rather the high life as a wealthy nobleman. He has no business whatsoever with straw.' Only wording nuance: the page never labels the phrase a 'simile' — that word is the claim's, not Pulley's; the comparison itself is quoted verbatim on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: It says volumes about both of them
verdicts.note: Quote exact and it is the last sentence of that paragraph, as the page hint says. The 'class histories' limb is carried by the page's own contrast in the immediately preceding sentences (stables → manservant vs King’s jester → wealthy nobleman), and the 'without statement' limb by 'says volumes' about an argument the page frames as being over 'this irrelevant woman'. The page does not use the word 'class'; it states the two social histories concretely.

verdicts.trueWording: but it has these pin-sharp moments too
verdicts.note: Quote exact, in the final body paragraph as the hint says: 'This trilogy has dragons in it, and prophets, and sweeping landscapes, but it has these pin-sharp moments too.' Every listed element (dragons, prophets, sweeping landscapes) and the contrast are on the page verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: admired the controlled point of view, the leisurely pace
verdicts.note: Raw page reached (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200); full essay body present. Quote exact: 'Started reading, admired the controlled point of view, the leisurely pace.' First-reading limb supported by the preceding paragraph ('I’d not read Hobb before and knew nothing of her'). Byline 'By Steven Erikson', 'Published on April 27, 2016'; bio on the page confirms novelist (Malazan Book of the Fallen).

verdicts.trueWording: deconstructing, line by line, to catch every subtle tell
verdicts.note: Quote exact. Both remaining limbs on the page in the same sentence and the one before it: 'that passage left me stunned, rapidly flipping back through the pages that led up to that scene. Rereading (I almost never reread), and then, in wonder, deconstructing, line by line, to catch every subtle tell, every hint that I missed the first time around.'

verdicts.trueWording: in the workshops I occasionally teach, I cite the opening chapters
verdicts.note: Quote exact: 'To this day in the workshops I occasionally teach, I cite the opening chapters of Assassin’s Apprentice as required reading when it comes to point of view.' All limbs supported. Two wording differences worth carrying if the sentence is quoted tightly: the page says 'cite ... as required reading' rather than 'sets', and 'workshops I occasionally teach' rather than an unqualified 'teaches'.

verdicts.trueWording: In our house, we have a galley, we have a head, we have a deck
verdicts.note: Raw page reached (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200); the Mike Barker transcript is on the episode page itself, lines attributed [Robin]. Quote exact, in the answer beginning 'Well, again, it’s knowing the character’s background', which also carries the farmer / sailing-ship vocabulary limb verbatim. Full passage: 'I’m married to a sailor. In our house, we have a galley, we have a head, we have a deck. I happen to have like a kitchen and a bathroom and a floor.' Two wording nuances: Hobb says 'we have' / 'I happen to have' rather than explicitly assigning the nautical terms to her husband (the sailor attribution is entailed by 'I’m married to a sailor', not stated), and deck/floor is not a room — 'the same rooms' is the claim's compression, not the transcript's.

verdicts.trueWording: you should be able to tell who is talking without all the little clues
verdicts.note: Quote exact: 'If you want to do a double check, read your dialogue. Can you tell by reading, not just a single line like a three word dialogue, but if there is a piece of dialogue and you read it, you should be able to tell who is talking without all the little clues like Joe said and Samantha replied.' The page hint's cue phrase is on the page and every limb (a test, read a passage of dialogue, tell the speaker without attribution tags) is supported; the episode's own homework repeats it ('examine the dialog itself, without tags').

verdicts.trueWording: Some characters speak in longer sentences, some speak in shorter sentences
verdicts.note: Quote exact, in the answer beginning 'If you have two farmers', as the hint says: 'If you have two farmers, a lot of it’s going to be based on attitude. Even the choice of sentence structure. If you think about it… I’m going to take The Lord of the Rings and think about how all the different characters in The Lord of the Rings, you can pretty much tell… Some characters speak in longer sentences, some speak in shorter sentences.' The Lord of the Rings limb is Hobb's own example, verbatim.
